body:
The conflict between Akbar and Mewar

During Akbar's reign, the Mughal Empire expanded through military campaigns as well as alliances with regional rulers. Several Rajput ruling houses entered Mughal service, but the Sisodiya rulers of Mewar continued to resist Mughal authority for a considerable period.

Maharana Pratap became the ruler of Mewar in 1572. He refused to submit to Akbar's authority. The resulting conflict led to the Battle of Haldighati on 18 June 1576.

Place and opposing sides

Haldighati is a mountain pass in the Aravalli region of present-day Rajsamand district, Rajasthan. The fighting is also associated with the nearby area of Khamnor.

  • Mewar side: Led by Maharana Pratap, supported by Mewar's chiefs and soldiers. The Afghan commander Hakim Khan Sur was among those who fought on Pratap's side, and Bhil supporters also contributed to his resistance.
  • Mughal side: An imperial army sent by Akbar and commanded by Raja Man Singh I of Amber.

The battle was therefore not simply a confrontation between soldiers belonging to 2 different religions. Rajput forces served on the Mughal side, and an Afghan commander fought alongside Maharana Pratap.

What was the result?

The Mughal army gained the advantage in the fighting and retained control of the battlefield. However, Maharana Pratap was not captured and Mewar did not submit permanently as a result of this single battle. Pratap withdrew and continued resistance from the difficult hill country.

The outcome is described differently in some regional accounts and commemorative traditions. Some emphasise that the battle was inconclusive because the Mughals failed to capture Pratap or secure his submission. For exam purposes, distinguish the immediate Mughal battlefield advantage from the failure to end Mewar's resistance.

Why the distinction matters

A military force may win control of a battlefield without achieving every political objective of its campaign. At Haldighati, the Mughal army was not able to turn its advantage into the capture of Maharana Pratap or his lasting acceptance of Mughal sovereignty. Pratap continued to struggle for control of Mewar.

Akbar was the Mughal emperor who ordered the campaign, but Raja Man Singh I of Amber commanded the Mughal army at Haldighati. Akbar did not personally lead the troops in this battle.

Prelims focus

  • Date: 18 June 1576.
  • Place: Haldighati, near Khamnor in present-day Rajasthan.
  • Mewar leader: Maharana Pratap.
  • Mughal commander: Raja Man Singh I of Amber.
  • Outcome: Mughal battlefield advantage; Maharana Pratap escaped and resistance continued.
  • Trap: Do not state that Akbar personally fought Maharana Pratap at Haldighati or that Mewar was permanently subdued in 1576.

[Sources: Rajasthan Tourism, Haldighati, consulted 19 November 2026; Rajasthan Board of Secondary Education, History and Culture of Rajasthan, Class 10, section on Maharana Pratap and the Battle of Haldighati; NIOS, Military History, Chapter 8, section 8.3, account of the Battle of Haldighati.]

pictures.alt: At Haldighati, the Mughals gained battlefield advantage, but Maharana Pratap was not captured and Mewar's resistance continued.
pictures.caption: Haldighati's immediate military outcome differed from its longer-term political outcome.

title: Battle of Haldighati (1576): Mughal Expansion and Mewar's Continued Resistance

body:
Why Gujarat mattered to the Mughals

Gujarat was an important political and commercial region. Its towns and ports connected inland markets with maritime trade. Akbar's campaigns in Gujarat aimed to bring this region under Mughal authority.

The Mughal conquest did not end with a single battle. Akbar obtained control of major centres in the early 1570s, but local rulers and supporters of the former Gujarat Sultanate continued to resist. The battles of Sarnal and Bhuchar Mori illustrate these different stages.

Battle of Sarnal, 1572

During the Gujarat campaign of 1572, Akbar encountered forces led by Ibrahim Husain Mirza, a rival military leader who controlled territory in Gujarat.

The confrontation occurred at Sarnal, near Thasra, near the Mahi River in the region of present-day Kheda district. Akbar defeated Ibrahim Husain Mirza, who escaped from the battlefield.

The victory helped Akbar overcome one of the important military challenges to his campaign in Gujarat. It should not be confused with either the Battle of Khanwa against Rana Sanga or the Battle of Haldighati against Maharana Pratap.

Gujarat becomes a Mughal province

Following Akbar's conquests, Gujarat became a Mughal subah, or province, in 1573. A subah was a major administrative division of the Mughal Empire governed on behalf of the emperor.

However, the establishment of a province did not automatically remove all resistance from local chiefs. Supporters of Muzaffar Shah III, the last ruler of the Gujarat Sultanate, continued to challenge Mughal control.

Battle of Bhuchar Mori, 1591

The Battle of Bhuchar Mori took place in 1591 near Dhrol in the Saurashtra region of present-day Jamnagar district.

  • Mughal side: Imperial forces under the Gujarat viceroy Mirza Aziz Koka, acting for Akbar.
  • Opposing side: A regional coalition supporting Muzaffar Shah III, including forces associated with Jam Sataji of Nawanagar and other local chiefs.
  • Result: Victory for Mughal forces and a major defeat for the coalition opposing Mughal authority.

Bhuchar Mori strengthened the Mughal hold over Gujarat and marked the effective end of the attempt to restore the old Gujarat Sultanate. The coalition included chiefs from different communities; describing the battle simply as a religious conflict would misrepresent the political alliances involved.

Conquest and consolidation are different stages

1572–1573 represents Akbar's initial conquest and establishment of Mughal provincial authority. 1591 represents a later military victory that strengthened that authority in Saurashtra. Keeping these stages separate helps explain why major battles could occur after Gujarat had formally become a Mughal province.

Prelims focus

  • Sarnal, 1572: Akbar defeated Ibrahim Husain Mirza near the Mahi River.
  • 1573: Gujarat became a Mughal subah.
  • Bhuchar Mori, 1591: Mughal forces defeated a coalition supporting Muzaffar Shah III.
  • Place: Bhuchar Mori is near Dhrol in Saurashtra.
  • Mughal commander at Bhuchar Mori: Mirza Aziz Koka.
  • Trap: The establishment of Gujarat as a Mughal province in 1573 did not mean that all regional resistance had ended by that year.

[Sources: The Cambridge History of India, Volume 4, section Operations against the Mirzas, printed p. 105; Gazetteer of the Bombay Presidency, Volume 1, Part 1, History of Gujarat, section Mughal Viceroys, account of Akbar's Gujarat campaign; Ahmedabad University, Bhuchar Mori: The Mughal Conquest of Gujarat and the Politics of Historical Narratives, seminar description by historian Aparna Kapadia, 26 March 2025.]

pictures.alt: Sarnal in 1572 and provincial status in 1573 mark Gujarat's conquest; Bhuchar Mori in 1591 marks later consolidation in Saurashtra.
pictures.caption: Two stages in establishing Mughal control over Gujarat.

title: Decisive Battles in Gujarat: Sarnal (1572) and Bhuchar Mori (1591)

body:
Why a war of succession began

In 1657, the illness of the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan created uncertainty about who would succeed him. His sons became involved in a struggle for the throne. The leading claimants included Dara Shikoh, Aurangzeb, Shah Shuja and Murad Baksh.

Dara Shikoh was Shah Jahan's eldest son and his favoured successor. Aurangzeb sought the throne with military support from Murad Baksh. The struggle was decided through a series of battles rather than by an uncontested transfer of power.

Battle of Dharmat, April 1658

The Battle of Dharmat was fought in April 1658 in the Malwa region, near present-day Ujjain in Madhya Pradesh.

The imperial army loyal to Shah Jahan and Dara Shikoh was commanded by Maharaja Jaswant Singh of Marwar and Qasim Khan. It confronted the combined forces of Aurangzeb and Murad Baksh.

Aurangzeb and Murad Baksh won. Their victory removed an important obstacle to their advance towards the Mughal capital.

Battle of Samugarh, 29 May 1658

The decisive confrontation followed at Samugarh, near Agra, on 29 May 1658. The principal opponents were:

  • Dara Shikoh: Leading forces defending his claim to succeed Shah Jahan.
  • Aurangzeb and Murad Baksh: Leading the opposing army.

Aurangzeb won the Battle of Samugarh. Dara Shikoh was forced to retreat. The defeat greatly weakened his claim and cleared the way for Aurangzeb's seizure of power.

After his victory, Aurangzeb took control of the imperial government and Shah Jahan was confined in Agra Fort. Samugarh was therefore a turning point in the Mughal war of succession. It was not a Mughal battle against an external invading empire.

Battle of Khajwa, January 1659

The struggle continued after Samugarh. In January 1659, Aurangzeb defeated his brother Shah Shuja at the Battle of Khajwa, also written as Khajuha, near Fatehpur in present-day Uttar Pradesh.

This victory weakened another rival claimant. The battles of Dharmat, Samugarh and Khajwa should therefore be understood as separate stages of the same struggle for the Mughal throne.

Gujarat connection

Before the war of succession, Murad Baksh was the Mughal governor of Gujarat. He joined Aurangzeb against the forces supporting Dara Shikoh. This links Gujarat directly to the struggle that led to Aurangzeb's accession.

Prelims focus

  • Dharmat, April 1658: Aurangzeb and Murad defeated imperial forces led by Jaswant Singh and Qasim Khan.
  • Samugarh, 29 May 1658: Aurangzeb and Murad defeated Dara Shikoh near Agra.
  • Khajwa, January 1659: Aurangzeb defeated Shah Shuja.
  • Gujarat connection: Murad Baksh was governor of Gujarat before joining Aurangzeb.
  • Trap: Samugarh was a war-of-succession battle between Mughal princes, not a war between the Mughals and the Marathas.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 4, The Mughal Empire, printed p. 49, 2020–21 edition; Maasir-i-Alamgiri, translated historical account, opening section on the Battle of Samugarh, 29 May 1658; Journal of the Royal Asiatic Society, Scrambling for Glory: Assessing True Rajput Identity in a Mughal War of Succession (1657–1659), 2026, discussion of Dharmat; Jadunath Sarkar, A Short History of Aurangzib, account of the succession battles.]

pictures.alt: Dharmat defeated imperial commanders, Samugarh defeated Dara Shikoh, and Khajwa defeated Shah Shuja, advancing Aurangzeb to the throne.
pictures.caption: The major military stages of the Mughal succession struggle of 1658–1659.

title: Samugarh (1658) and the Battles of Mughal Succession

body:
The changing political situation after Aurangzeb

Aurangzeb died in 1707. The later Mughal Empire experienced succession struggles, growing independence of provincial governors and challenges from regional powers. The expansion of Maratha influence and invasions from outside India further weakened effective Mughal authority.

The battles of Jajau, Palkhed and Karnal illustrate 3 different kinds of conflict: a contest for the imperial throne, a regional struggle involving the Marathas and the Nizam, and a foreign invasion of the Mughal Empire.

Battle of Jajau, 1707

The Battle of Jajau took place in June 1707 near Agra. It was fought between 2 sons of Aurangzeb who claimed the Mughal throne:

  • Prince Muazzam: The future emperor Bahadur Shah I.
  • Prince Azam Shah: A rival claimant to the throne.

Prince Muazzam won and subsequently ruled as Bahadur Shah I. Jajau was another Mughal succession battle, but it occurred after Aurangzeb's death rather than during Shah Jahan's lifetime.

Battle of Palkhed, 1728

The Battle of Palkhed in 1728 was part of a campaign between Peshwa Baji Rao I, representing Maratha power, and Nizam-ul-Mulk, the powerful ruler of Hyderabad.

Baji Rao I emerged victorious. The Maratha campaign forced the Nizam to accept an agreement favourable to the Marathas. The result demonstrated the growing strength of the Marathas during a period when Mughal control over regional powers was declining.

Palkhed is particularly associated with Baji Rao's successful campaign of manoeuvre. It should not be confused with the Third Battle of Panipat, where a later Maratha army was defeated by Ahmad Shah Abdali.

Battle of Karnal, 1739

The Battle of Karnal was fought on 24 February 1739 near Karnal in present-day Haryana.

  • Invading side: Nadir Shah, ruler of Persia, or Iran.
  • Mughal side: Forces of the Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah.
  • Result: Nadir Shah won a decisive victory.

Following the defeat, Nadir Shah advanced to Delhi and plundered the city in 1739. The invasion exposed the military weakness of the later Mughal state and further damaged its political authority.

Why the names must be kept separate

Nadir Shah, who defeated the Mughals at Karnal in 1739, was the ruler of Persia. Ahmad Shah Abdali, also known as Ahmad Shah Durrani, was an Afghan ruler who later defeated the Marathas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Their victories occurred in different years against different opponents.

Prelims focus

  • Jajau, 1707: Prince Muazzam defeated Azam Shah and became Bahadur Shah I.
  • Palkhed, 1728: Baji Rao I defeated Nizam-ul-Mulk.
  • Karnal, 1739: Nadir Shah defeated Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah's forces.
  • 1739: Nadir Shah plundered Delhi after his victory.
  • Trap: Nadir Shah at Karnal in 1739 and Ahmad Shah Abdali at Panipat in 1761 were different rulers.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–II, Class 7, Chapter 10, Eighteenth-Century Political Formations, printed pp. 139–150, 2020–21 edition; Cambridge University Press, historical account of Mughal succession after Aurangzeb, discussion of Jajau, June 1707; The Maratha Supremacy, section Disruption of the Mughal Empire, printed p. 121, account of Palkhed; Encyclopaedia Iranica, India VII: Relations in the Afsharid and Zand Periods, account of Nadir Shah's invasion and Karnal.]

pictures.alt: Timeline distinguishes internal Mughal succession at Jajau, Maratha victory at Palkhed, and Persian invasion at Karnal followed by Delhi's plunder.
pictures.caption: Three different challenges to political power in early 18th-century India.

title: Jajau, Palkhed and Karnal (1707–1739): Succession, Regional Power and Foreign Invasion
